extracted.intended_audience: communication researchers, journalism educators, and graduate students in mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply criteria for high-quality mass communication research, educational-media program design/evaluation, and development communication; emphasizes theoretical paradigms, empirical rigor, practical utility, and cross-cultural sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Shannon-Weaver transmission model
rubrics_metrics.description: Schramm's transliteration of the Shannon-Weaver transmission model (source-encoder-signal-decoder-destination) as a pervasive conceptual paradigm for analyzing mass communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the transmission model as one of the core conceptual tools for structuring communication research — explicit mapping of source, encoding, signal, decoding, and destination helps frame empirical studies. Use it alongside human-centered models rather than as sole explanatory device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt motivational and learning-theory paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret communication phenomena using motivational and learning theory (e.g., Schramm's characterization that people 'select news in expectation of a reward' and the distinction between immediate and delayed reward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify content and audience uses by reward type: immediate reward (crime, accidents, sports, human interest) versus delayed reward (public affairs, economics, science, education, health). Use these distinctions to predict selection and attention patterns and to design studies of media effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate news by 'immediate reward' vs 'delayed reward' categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Schramm's taxonomy: immediate reward news (crime, corruption, accidents, sports, social events, human interest) and delayed reward news (public affairs, economic matters, social problems, science, education, health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing news content or audience selection, code stories into these categories to interpret motivations for attention and potential learning outcomes; be aware of normative judgments that may accompany such labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize effects on individuals and learning outcomes over hardware
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational-media work should focus 'not on the hardware or the process but on what happens to the individuals involved, on the expansion of opportunities' and making learning more available, exciting and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate media interventions primarily by measures of learner outcomes (knowledge, attitudes, behavior, access), not by novelty of technology. Avoid introducing technology 'for its own sake.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge experimentation and practical utilization (action-orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should 'bridge the gap between experimentation and practical utilization' — be oriented to action and solving real problems rather than being purely theoretical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include implementation-focused components (feasibility, scalability, policy relevance) and involve practitioners and planners so findings can inform real educational or development programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple measures and rigorous evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schramm's projects (e.g., Stanford–Denver Spanish TV project, Colombia Peace Corps evaluation) exemplify using 'multiple measures' and careful evaluation to assess media-based educational innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ multi-method evaluation designs (pre/post tests, control/comparison groups, behavioral measures, longitudinal follow-up) and report limitations candidly; triangulate across measures to support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, realistic appraisal of educational-media programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct 'realistic appraisal' and honest assessments of educational-media initiatives; avoid overstated claims about impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both successes and failures; base recommendations on evidence; perform cross-national surveys and case studies to understand contextual constraints and realistic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess media effects in terms of social functions and collective responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate media effects by their societal functions — e.g., Schramm's analysis of the Kennedy assassination response emphasized sharing of common information, reassertion of national norms, national mourning as catharsis, and focus of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying major events or media phenomena, analyze not only individual-level outcomes but also collective functions (rituals, norms reinforcement, collective coping) and differing cultural responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize literature to define field boundaries and guide practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Schramm's edited readers and handbooks (Mass Communications, Process and Effects, The Science of Human Communication, Handbook of Communication) function as devices to 'define the boundaries and the substance of the field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce or use comprehensive syntheses and accessible texts to orient newcomers; value integrative work that collects seminal studies and frames research agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-media and cross-modal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct 'instructional cross-media comparisons' and case studies to determine relative effectiveness of media forms for educational purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comparative studies that hold content constant while varying media delivery to isolate media-specific effects; document contextual variables affecting each medium's performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary collaboration with educators, planners, and behavioral scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek 'cross-fertilization with educators' and coordinate with planners and behavioral scientists to ensure relevance and uptake of research findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage stakeholders (school administrators, curriculum planners, policy-makers) in study design and interpretation; tailor measures to decision-makers' needs (e.g., administrative feasibility, cost, training requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about theoretical grand unification; ground claims empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Schramm's historical commentary notes that early optimism about converging grand theories faded; theories may not converge and empirical complexity persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on a single grand theory; prioritize empirically driven hypotheses, replication, and attention to boundary conditions and contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess transferability of development-communication lessons across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Question 'How transferrable is [one country's] experience?' (e.g., China's experience) — development communication insights require scrutiny before transplanting across national contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cultural, institutional, and infrastructural differences; use pilot studies and local adaptation rather than direct replication; include indigenous stakeholders in planning and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider scalability, financing and institutional arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning and assessment should include financing and institutional aspects (e.g., reports on 'The Financing of Public Television', building communication institutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cost analysis, funding models, and institutional capacity assessments in program design and evaluation; consider sustainability and long-term integration into existing systems.
